meta.title: Amazon kept shutting down my tablet, so I spent $266 on four AI models to own it

comments.author: Tiraon
comments.text:
The problem here is legal which was apparently solved by technical means .

Manufacturers are somehow allowed to sell devices that they still maintain control of. Having unrecoverable bugs, completely bricking the device or changing core functions even years after the fact is perfectly normal and they never face any meaningfull consequences. And their ability to do this is legally protected and the owners ability to evade it and maintain actual ownership over their legally purchased property is legally dubious to nonexistant.

This is only possible due to the abysmal computer literacy rates. The dismissive attitude towards having trivial level knowledge about something that drives majority of someones life never ceases to amaze me.

comments.author: carsonc
comments.text:

comments.author: post_below
comments.text: The price doesn't have to be that high, a $100  subscription with a top lab would have handled all of the devices the author tested with and dozens more before the month was out.

comments.author: sparkle
comments.text:
I know the author didn't need to and this was mostly an exercise in just "what can I actually do" and I agree that you should be allowed to root and own your device, but I can't help but wonder - why not just block the tablet from external connections?

The author mentioned using adguard home initially which makes me think they tried. The errors and the package names seem to indicate OTA is at least partially behind the shutdowns. But if they're just using it to display home assistant 24/7, presumably locally hosted, why not just give a static address to the tablet and some firewall rules to block it from non-internal access?

I did exactly this after I found out that my Kindle Paperwhite was phoning home to an unnamed EC2 instance and used direct IP connections as a fallback if DNS failed. I didn't trust the OTA block utilities provided with WinterBreak or other scripts - they just move or rename the updater binary and I don't want my device to contact Amazon servers ever (or anybody else's either), I just want it to be able to access local resources like calibre and kosync.

At the end of the day, it is neat to root your own previously unrooted device and I imagine the author learned a lot along the way and most importantly, enjoyed themselves. Rooting and uninstalling everything surely felt good and also definitively prevents future reoccurrences.  And maybe the author did block it, but the shutdowns continued and just didn't mention it.

I wonder what Louis Rossman would have to say about this...

comments.author: PraiseTheSoup
comments.text: Interesting read. I agree that based on principles it had to be done. However, I personally could never have spent that much time and money on it.

comments.author: Prodiggles
comments.text:
Big win is really for the next person that comes along that falls into the same situation, this person may have saved them a bunch of time trying to even figure out feasibility.

So, we have a pass-it-forward model on the backs of those that felt it was important to spend resources on, and we can hope to have the same outcome for more device models in the future.

I do occasionally find neat things like this and when it objectively saves me time I have no problem sending them a $5 for a coffee to say thanks, remembering this was a person (even if using AI to do it) that put their effort into trying to make it easier on them and others in the future.

comments.author: teaearlgraycold
comments.text: It might be illegal to distribute patches for devices, but I doubt it would be illegal to distribute a prompt that has been verified to achieve a certain outcome when used with a certain LLM. This will be an interesting development for game console jailbreaking in particular. You’re sold hardware at cost or at a loss only because the manufacturer expects to keep you in a walled garden.

comments.author: PendingKetchup
comments.text: Do you understand the DMCA angle here? The author keeps saying that this is all perfectly legal because of a DMCA exemption, and they link to like the homepage about DMCA exemptions, but why would one even be needed? They're exploiting a security hole to get root and then issuing a bunch of package uninstallation commands. They're not circumventing any copy protection mechanisms, are they? "Not having root on a tablet" is hardly an effective technical copy protection measure, right?

comments.author: teaearlgraycold
comments.text: Well Kindles let you buy DRM'd ebooks. Rooting circumvents that DRM.

comments.author: PendingKetchup
comments.text: Doesn't circumventing the DRM require having some kind of software that would actually capture, copy, or decrypt protected content, rather than just convincing the device to follow your instructions? One is a necessary step to the other, but so is, say, attaching the USB cable.

comments.author: CrypticCuriosity629
comments.text:
Honestly this is awesome because I have a Fire Tab, slightly older gen than the one in the article, and I too use it purely with Fully kiosk Browser, but I use it to monitor and control my 3D Printers.

I've had to retire it recently because despite unlocking as much as I could with ADB and some Fire Tab tools from XDA, Amazon consistently bloated the tablet with so much background BS it was basically useless.

I had to run an automated script that force closed everything every 30 minutes.

It sucks because it's a nice tablet and I see exactly how much capability it has if I could juts debloat it.

I'll have to compare mine to theirs and see if I can gleen anything from their work.

comments.text: I wonder how the software situation is on Walmart’s Onn brand tablets? I’ve been hearing good things about them lately.

comments.author: Carrow
comments.text:
I just bought one of the 2026 4K streaming sticks. It's Android TV, no extra software beyond what Google puts on, almost like Pixel of streaming. The default Google TV launcher has an ad plastered front and center and is bloated with Gemini, Live "TV", stuff like that. But you can install other launchers and reprogram the buttons so you never go to that launcher. No side loading, abd, or root required. They are rootable if you stop it from applying a patch over the internet on first boot.

I assume it's similar for their tablets.
